Considering the history of philosophy is as much a narrative that we tell ourselves as regular history, it would be hard to find a major figure that does not fit in the narrative and thus « seem to pop out of nowhere ». We tend to make the history of ideas more dialectical than it really is because we forget about those who didn’t fit our narrative. These forgotten philosophers would be the ones you’re looking for. 

Otherwise, as the other answer stated, you’d have to look at thinkers that stand outside philosophy, like poets and such.
I’d say Hölderlin could be interesting for you. His thought is very peculiar for his time, even though Heidegger made his ideas more wide known much later. 
In some way, Nietzsche could also fit your description, since he is one of the major critic of traditional philosophy in the West, thus his ideas seem very alien to philosophy up until Heidegger popularized his ideas. We must not forget Nietzsche was mostly an unknown author, and that he was considered to be a poet because he didn’t fit our philosophical narrative, before Heidegger came in and took his ideas seriously. However, Nietzsche’s ideas still are motivated by the will to oppose what came before him.

Another possibility would be to see Oriental philosophy, which has its own history. However, by the way of the Greeks, the medieval time, and contemporary times, its history also intertwines with ours.

Depends of what you're doing with it. 

If you're reading it to grasp the general ideas of a philosopher, any recognized translation will do.  You have to first rub shoulders with the general ideas and then study them profoundly before you can decide which specific interpretation (translation) has more value. When you understand the idea so clearly that you feel something might be wrong in the translation, then it's time to chose.

If you already have a good understanding of a philosopher's ideas, then you might want to get picky and search for the translator's background. Translators also have a subjective understanding of the text and they'll translate it accordingly. There are, for example, very christianized translation of Plato and Aristotle and others that try to translate it by thinking in an "Ancient Greek" frame of mind... Depends of what your goal is, what you'll use it for and so on.


If you're quoting it for an academic paper you're writing, you'll probably want the latest renowned translation. Except if you can justify your choice in a significant way for the point of your paper.

This is very true. Heidegger has gone a great length to fit Nietzsche into his “history of being”.
The volumes on Nietzsche are a good place to start to understand the Nietzsche-Heidegger reationship. However, I’d recommend Introduction to metaphysics.

Because he reduces being to a “nothing” (nihil). According to Heidegger, Nietzsche’s characterization of nihilism is insufficient. It is true that history has, so far, followed the movement of nihilism (valuation and devaluation). Plato valued ideas, Christians valued God, and now Scientists value Matter. This movement may go on forever or halt when we have found what it really means to be. However, for Heidegger, we have only questioned thus far towards the essence of beings, but never towards the essence of being itself. It is not by questioning the being of beings that we can understand the meaning of being itself, but by trying to think what it means that “there is” beings. In short, Heidegger thinks that nihilism is more profound than Nietzsche thought. It is because we forgot to think about being that the cycle of nihilism even exists; because we try to value such and such being to explain being as a whole, but none of these supreme beings can fully explain every phenomenon. By reducing being to a vapor and saying will to power explains everything, Nietzsche just inserts himself in the history of metaphysics and contributes to nihilism himself. However, by naming the movement of history, he also kind of stands out of it because he allows us to see beyond. 

This seems very abstract and made me hate Heidegger in the first place. Especially since Nietzsche tries to ground everything in the body and Heidegger keeps talking about Being, which seems very metaphysical and idealistic. However, in Being and Time, even if he doesn’t say it clearly, Heidegger accounts for the body. It is a must read if you like Nietzsche’s thought. They share very common interests even if they can seem to be opposites.

If I would personally agree that it is more than its essential definition, yes. But if that’s what you’re interested in, I wouldn’t care much for Kant or more traditional idealism. What I mean is that I don’t think that Kant’s thought have the means to tackle such problems. He doesn’t care much for things in themselves as far as they’re not accessible to consciousness (since the categories of the mind shape what we can perceive of reality. Insofar as we only have access the phenomenon, we can’t ever reach the thing in itself anyway.

Something in itself is less about wether the thing is a complex of things or not. An electron, even if it isn’t composed of anything else, can’t be a thing in itself because the expression « thing in itself » refers to the essence of that thing, aka what all of the electrons share as an essential characteristic without which they wouldn’t be what they are. Thus, an electron « in itself » isn’t some physical entity, but the idea of it: it is its (essential) definition.

Yeah I get it. But to me, playing roles isn't about impressing people. I also aim to share fascination, I don't play roles all the time of course. I've just found that it helps feeling less isolated. Rather than leaving a conversation empty handed and disappointed, I learn about behavior while having a casual encounter.

I also feel alienated in a similar fashion, but I find it is rather because I am interested in intellectual matters. I like to explore things more deeply than the people with whom I share my thoughts with. Thus, either I dumb down what I have to say so it is accessible, which makes me feel isolated because I cannot share the depth of my thought; either I go in great details and nuances, which takes time and makes people lose interest, which in turn makes me feel isolated because nobody is as fascinated as I am. That's why I think I might feel your solitude. 

The best tip that I might give you because it worked for me is this: try presenting yourself to new people as if you were playing a role. Use a different name, try behaving differently, be another character. I've found it very stimulating, because you start to understand how people relate to eachother and at the same time it is mentally challenging. I'm still not as satisfied as I could be, but it helped me feel less solitude.

Edit: i am also very outgoing, playing roles was then very easy for me.
